full_judgment:
4. In the application, it was contended, inter alia, that after the enactment of the Durnity Daman Commission Ain, 2004 (the Ain, 2004,) the initiation of any proceeding in respect of any offence described in the schedule thereto prior sanction of the Durnity Daman Commission (the Commission) under section 32 of the Ain, 2004 was necessary, but in the instant case, no such prior sanction was taken and the Senior Special Judge without seeking any sanction of the Commission also took cognizance of the offence against the petitioner; even under the repealed provisions of sub-section (5) of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 (the Act, 1958) before taking cognizance, the Special Judge, first of all, was required to comply with the provisions thereof by addressing letter to the Government immediately on receipt of the police report to accord , sanction to prosecute the accused if the police report were not accompanied by such sanction, but in the instant case, the learned Senior Special Judge look cognizance of the offence without writing any letter either to the Government or to the Commission though the police report did not accompany such sanction letter. Therefore, continuation of the impugned proceedings was nothing but an abuse of the process of the Court; the instant criminal proceeding is unjust as a civil suit being Money Suit No. 1 of 2005 is pending where liability of the petitioner will be determined and the issues being almost identical and same, in both the civil and the criminal case, there is every chance of conflicting decision if the criminal case is allowed to proceed; after-acceptance of the police report on 3-11-2004 by the Magistrate, the petitioner was deemed to have been discharged and unless the order of discharge was set-aside by a competent Court, fresh order of taking cognizance by the Senior Special Judge in the self-same case was illegal and unjustified and, as such, the impugned proceeding was an abuse of the process of the Court and the same was liable to be quashed. 

 6. Mr ASM Abdul Mobin, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that the High Court Division found that the Senior Special Judge did not find any support of the confessional statement of accused Farid Uddin as to the complicity of Nasir Chowdhury and Ahmed Chowdhury, who were not sent up in the charge-sheet along with the petitioner, erred factually and legally in not quashing the impugned proceedings so far as it relates to the petitioner. He has further submitted that the learned Senior Special Judge took cognizance of the offence against the petitioner on mere guess that he as Manager of the bank had an obligation to look after the day to day work of the bank and check the misappropriation of the money of the bank though he stood on the same footing with other persons, namely: Nasiruddin Chowdhury and Ahmed Chowdhury Mr Mobin has further submitted that though section 6(5) of the Act, 1958 was repealed on 18-5-2004, the sanction for prosecuting the petitioner either under the repealed law or under the new law, was necessary and since the police report did not accompany such sanction, the learned Senior Special Judge was under an obligation to write to the Commission to give sanction to prosecute the petitioner, instead he took cognizance of the offence under section 409 of the Penal Code straightaway and thus acted illegally and without jurisdiction, the learned Judges of the High Court Division on a wrong approach as to the effect of repealing of sub-section (5) of section 6 of the Act, 1958 on 18-5-2004 erroneously held that prior sanction of the Government for prosecuting the petitioner, was not necessary and that the Senior Special Judge committed no illegality in taking cognizance of the offence against the petitioner. He has further submitted that section 32 of the Ain, 2004 has made it mandatory to have sanction of the Commission to take cognizance of an offence under the Ain, 2004 and section 409 of the Penal Code being an offence in the schedule to the Ain, which came into force on 9-5-2004, the Senior Special judge acted illegally and without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence against the petitioner on 12-3-2005, i.e. long after coming into force of the Ain, 2004 without any sanction from the Commission on the view that section 409 of the Penal Code is not an offence under the Ain, but mentioned in the schedule thereto and that there is clear difference between the offences under the Ain and the offences under other laws mentioned in the schedule thereto. He has further submitted that the High Court Division was absolutely wrong in holding that section 38 of the Ain, 2004 has no manner of application in the case as the offence under section 409 of the Penal Code was not an offence under the repealed Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 (the Act, 1957), which was repealed by the said section and this wrong view has resulted in an erroneous decision in discharging the Rule. He has lastly submitted that in the instant case, though FIR was lodged on 17-12-2003, the case was pending for investigation when the Ain, 2004 came into force on 9-5-2004 and after the coming into force of the Ain, 2004, the police or any other agency had no authority to proceed with the investigation of the case in view of sub-section (1) of section 20 thereof, the continuation of investigation of the case by the police was without jurisdiction and the report submitted by the police was no report in the eye of law and there-fore, taking cognizance of the offence by the Senior Special Judge on such police report was illegal and without jurisdiction and, as such, continuation of the impugned proceeding is nothing but an abuse of the process of the Court and the same is liable to be quashed. 

 (iii) Whether prior sanction of the Government or of the Commission was necessary to take cognizance of the offence under section 409 of the Penal Code against the petitioner by the Senior Special Judge in view of the repeal of section 6(5) of the Act, 1958 on 18-5-2004 by Act, XXII of 2004. 

 12. Sub-section (3) of section 38 is the saving provision and in this sub-section, it has been clearly provided that the enquiry, investigation of a case and the process of giving sanction to start a case under the Act, 1957, which were pending immediately before the repeal thereof, shall be completed by the Commission under the provisions of Ain, 2004. The language of sub-section (3) of section 38 is so clear that it does not admit of any ambiguity. The only thing to be seen is whether section 409 of the penal Code was an offence under the Act, 1957. In the whole of the Act, 1957, neither the offence has been defined nor has it been stated that the offence means the offence under the Act. In sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Act, it has been clearly stipulated that notwithstanding anything contained in the Police Act, 1861, the Government may constitute a Bureau for enquiry into and investigation of the offences specified in the schedule thereto and the offences notified by the Government. Sub-section (2) has provided that subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf, the Officers of the Bureau shall have throughout the country in relation to the inquiry into, and investigation of, such offences, all powers of seizure, search and arrest of persons concerned in such offences and all other powers, duties, privileges and liabilities, which the police officers have in connection with the investigation of such offences. Sub-section (3) has provided that notwithstanding anything contained in the Code, any Officers of the Bureau may, subject to any orders which the Government may make in this behalf; exercise any of the powers of an Officer-in-Charge of a police station in the area in which he is for the time being and when so exercising such powers shall subject to any such orders as aforesaid, be deemed to be an Officer-in-Charge of a police station discharging the functions of such an officer within the limits of his station. And pursuant to the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 3, a schedule has been appended to the Act, 1957 and in clause (c) of the schedule, section 409 of the Penal Code has clearly been mentioned (in the schedule of the Act, 1957, in the book published by Dhaka Law Reports under the title as 'The Special Powers Act and Anti-Corruption Commission Act with some other allied laws, Eight Edition, 2007; section 409 of the Penal Code has not been printed, but in the East Pakistan Code, sections 403 to 409 of the Penal Code, have been clearly mentioned in the schedule. We have checked whether section 409 of the Penal Code was omitted subsequently from the schedule of the Act, 1957, but we have not found any such omission. It may be stated that in sections 4 and 5 of the Act, 1957, some offences have been contemplated and the punishments for commission of such offences have also been provided there; in the schedule, in clause (a), it has been mentioned "Offences under this Act," offences under other laws have been mentioned from clauses (b) to (j). From the impugned judgment, it appears that the learned Judges took the view that as the offence under section 409 of the Penal Code was not an offence under the Act, 1957, but specified in the schedule thereto, the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 38 of the Ain, 2004 was not applicable. The learned Judges took the further view that the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 38 of the Ain, 2004 was applicable only in respect of the cases under the Act, 1957 which were "under enquiry, investigation and pending for sanction" immediately before the repealing of the Act. In holding so, the learned Judges gave stress on the words "Offences under this Act" as specified in clause (a) of the schedule to the Act, 1957. The learned Judges totally failed to consider that schedule to the Act, 1957 was appended pursuant to section 3(1) of the Act. To us it appears that the words "Offences under this Act" were mentioned in the schedule as some offences were contemplated in sections 4 and 5 of the Act and punishments for such offences were also provided there. And, if in the schedule to the Act, 1957 "Offences under this Act" would not have been mentioned, the offences as contemplated in sections 4 and 5 of the Act, 1957, would have been left out of the purview of enquiry into an investigation by the Bureau, because of the language used in the sub-section (1) of section 3. And such an omission would have created a serious contradiction in between sections 3(1), 4 and 5 of the Act and the schedule appended thereto and would have also created confusion in the mind of the investigating authority, namely: the Bureau to enquire and investigate about the offences contemplated in sections 4 and 5 of the Act, 1957. Schedule appended to a statute cannot be isolated from the statute, particularly, when the same is appended pursuant to the provisions of the statute, here section 3(1) of the Act, 1957, so it must be treated as a part of the statute. In interpreting the words/ expression or a terminology used in a particular section of a statute or in the schedule appended thereto, the other provisions of the statute have to be taken into consideration so that such interpretation cannot make any part or provision of the statute meaningless, nugatory and ineffective. A cohesive reading of sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act, 1957 with the schedule thereto, it appears to us that the whole object of the legislature behind the enactment of the Act, was to enquire into and investigate of the offences effectively under sections 4 and 5 of the Act, 1957 and also under other laws as specified in the schedule thereto by the Bureau. And section 409 of the Penal Code being in the schedule to the Act, 1957, it was definitely a part thereof and an offence under the Act. Therefore, the learned Judges were absolutely wrong in holding that sub-section (3) of section 38 of the Ain, 2004 was not applicable in respect of the investigation of the instant case as section 409 of the Penal Code was not an offence under the Act, 1957. 

 15. From a reading of original section 32 of the Ain, 2004 shows that necessity of prior sanction of the Commission in order to file a case in respect of an offence under the Ain was mandatory and it was also mandatory to file a copy of the sanction of the Commission at the time of filing the case. And except original section 32 as quoted hereinbefore, there was no other provision in the Ain, 2004 as to the necessity of the sanction of the Commission for taking cognizance of an offence under the Ain, 2004 by a Special Judge. It is needless to mention that the Act, 1958 was enacted for more speedy trial and more effective punishments of certain offences and the petitioner and the other accused being bank officials are public servants and the offence allegedly committed by them being under section 409 of the Penal Code was exclusively cognizable and tribale by the Special Judge under the Act, 1958. Section 6(5) of the Act, 1958 clearly provided that notwithstanding anything contained in the Code or any other law, previous sanction of the Government shall be required for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence under the Act, and such, sanction shall be sufficient for the prosecution of a public servant for an offence tribale under the act. The section further provided that in case, where the complaint or report referred in sub-section (1) of section 4 of the Act, 1958 was not accompanied by such sanction, the special judge shall, immediately, on receipt of the complaint or report, address, by letter, to the Government, in the matter, and if the required sanction is neither received nor refused within sixty days of the receipt of the letter by the Government, such sanction shall be deemed to have been duly accorded. This provision was repealed on 18-5-2004 by Act, XX11 of 2004. This was repealed rightly because with the coming into force of the Ain, 2004 on 9-5-2004,the Act, 1957 by which the Bureau was created to enquire into, and investigate of, offences relating to corruption and subsequently, inserted words "and certain other offences" by Act 1 of 1974 and for making provisions for enquiry into the pecuniary resources of certain persons for more effective prevention of corruption stood repealed on 9-5-2004. And after the repeal of the Act, the Government could not have any control in any manner whatsoever over the Commission which would in effect destroy its independence. When the FIR was lodged by the police on 17-12-2003 giving rise to the instant case, original section 32 of the Ain, 2004 was not in existence, so the question of application of original section 32 to the instant case does not arise at all. Original section 32 was substituted on 18th April, 2007 by Act, VII of 2007. In sub-section (1) of the substituted section 32, it has been provided that notwithstanding anything contained in the code or any other law for the time being in force, no Court shall take cognizance of any offence under the Ain, 2004 without the sanction of the Commission. Sub-section (2) of the section has further provided that after completion of investigation of an offence under the Ain, 2004 and before submission of the report the investigation officer shall obtain prior sanction of the Commission and a copy of such sanction of the Commission shall be filed with the report. 

 17. In section 17, the functions of the Commission have been enumerated. In clause (ক) thereof, it has been clearly stated that the enquiry into and the investigation of offences mentioned in the schedule to the Ain, 2004 shall be conducted by the Commission. Therefore, it would be an absurd interpretation that no prior sanction of the Commission would be required in taking cognizance of an offence mentioned in the schedule to the Ain, 2004 by the Special Judge as provided in sub-section (1) of section 32 and that no sanction would be required before submitting any report by the investigation officer after completion of investigation of the offences mentioned in the schedule to the AM as provided in sub-section (2) of section 32 other than the offences under the Ain, 2004. If the view of the High Court Division is accepted, it will give an anomalous situation. Not only that another authority has to be established to give sanction to take cognizance by the Special Judge constituted under the Act, 1958 and also to give sanction for submission of the report by the investigation officer in respect of the offences under other laws mentioned in the schedule to the Ain, 2004 within the meaning of substituted section 32, though those offences shall be enquired into and investigated by the Commission or by any of its authorized officer, as presently there is no such other authority. In this regard, clause (ঞ) of section 17 of the Ain, 2004 may also be referred to which shows that one of the functions of the Commission is to prescribe the procedure as to the sanction to be given by it in respect of the enquiry, investigation and filing of a case in relation to corruption. Neither in clause (ক) nor in clause (ঞ) of section 17, any difference has been made about the offences under the Ain, 2004 nor the offences under other laws mentioned in the schedule to the Ain. Then, how come that without sanction of the Commission the Special Judge shall take cognizance of an offence under other laws mentioned in the schedule to the Ain, 2004 and the investigation officer shall submit his report without the sanction of the Commission as well. 

 24. The learned Judges further held that since sub-section (5) of section 6 of the Act. 1958 was repealed on 18-4-2004 by Act XXII of 2004, therefore" at the time of submission of police report, on 29-10-2004 prior sanction of the Government for prosecuting the accused was not required under the law in existence." So, taking of cognizance of the offence under section 409 of the Penal Code against the petitioner by the Senior Special Judge on 12-3-2005 in the absence of any sanction was not illegal or without lawful authority. In view of our findings that continuation of the investigation of the case in question by the police after coming into force of the Ain, 2004 was illegal and without jurisdiction, the question as to whether prior sanction of the Government or the Commission was required for taking cognizance by the Senior Special fudge against the petitioner in view of the repeal of sub-section (5) of section 6 of the Act, 1958 as formulated in question No.(iii) has become academic in view of the substituted section 32 of the Ain, 2004 as discussed earlier, therefore, we are not inclined to waste our time in deliberating upon the same. As we have held that the report submitted by the police under section 173 of the Code on the basis of which the learned Special Judge took cognizance of the offence against the petitioner was not a report in the eye of law, now there is no other alternative but to get the case investigated afresh by the Commission, no answer to question No.(v) is called for.
